practice_description.medium: robotic drawing, performance, installation, sculpture, AI collaboration, biosensing
practice_description.practice_summary: Artist and researcher pioneering human-machine collaboration through the D.O.U.G. (Drawing Operations Unit Generation) series — custom-built robotic systems that co-draw with the artist. The artwork IS the feedback loop between human gesture and machine response, making relational composition between human and non-human agents the primary medium.
practice_description.methodology: Chung designs and builds successive generations of collaborative robotic systems, each exploring a different dimension of human-machine relation: mimicry (computer vision tracking hand gestures), memory (RNNs trained on decades of the artist's drawings), collectivity (swarm robots trained on urban surveillance data), spectrality (EEG biofeedback translating meditative states into robotic movement). The artistic process is performative — Chung draws alongside the robots in real-time, creating a live feedback loop where each agent responds to the other's marks. Errors and unpredictable machine behaviors are embraced as creative contributions ('poeticize error'). Founded Scilicet studio (2019) to further explore human and non-human collaboration across robotics, bio-sensing, and interspecies technologies.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Chung's practice is the most direct demonstration of relational composition as medium — the artwork emerges from the real-time feedback loop between human and machine agents. This models exactly how a Sense Room could operate: multiple agents (human visitors, algorithmic systems, data feeds) co-composing an exhibition in real-time through their interactions.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Partially. The drawn/painted outputs serve as material traces of the collaborative process — substrate that records the relational dynamic. However, the primary artwork is the performative process itself rather than the static output.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Yes, fundamentally. The entire practice IS relational composition. The artwork emerges exclusively from the feedback loop between human and machine — neither agent alone produces the result. Each D.O.U.G. generation explores a different relational modality (mimicry, memory, collectivity, spectrality).
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Yes. The robotic systems respond in real-time to the artist's gestures (and vice versa), creating continuously evolving compositions. D.O.U.G._4 (Spectrality) recomposes based on the artist's brainwave data. The swarm systems (D.O.U.G._3) self-organize in response to environmental inputs.

works.title: Drawing Operations (D.O.U.G._1: Mimicry)
works.description: First generation: open-source robotic arm with computer vision that mirrors the artist's drawing gestures in real-time. Small errant movements create unpredictable creative deviations.
works.relevance: Foundational demonstration of human-machine co-authorship through relational feedback. The embrace of error as creative force models how A(DAI)'s system could incorporate unpredictable emergent behaviors.

works.title: MEMORY (D.O.U.G._2)
works.description: Robotic system driven by recurrent neural network trained on two decades of the artist's digitized drawings. Acquired by the V&A (2022) — first AI model in a major museum collection — comprising print, film, and RNN model in 3D printed sculpture.
works.relevance: Demonstrates how a machine can internalize an artist's practice as training data and become a collaborative agent. The V&A acquisition validates AI co-authorship within institutional art frameworks.

works.title: Spectral
works.description: Performative installation at the World Economic Forum. Robotic painting arms driven by real-time EEG biofeedback from the artist's brainwaves, translating meditative states into painterly movements on transparent canvas.
works.relevance: Most advanced expression of the feedback loop concept — internal states (brain activity) directly drive relational composition with robotic agents, demonstrating how invisible data (like graph relationships) could drive visible artistic output.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Chung treats the design of human-machine collaborative protocols as the artistic medium itself. Each D.O.U.G. generation defines a different protocol for interaction between human and machine agents. The rules governing the feedback loop — how gesture is sensed, interpreted, and responded to — ARE the artwork. Scilicet studio extends this to interspecies protocols.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Five generations of D.O.U.G. collaborative drawing systems, each defining a distinct human-machine interaction protocol. Scilicet studio as a research infrastructure for developing new forms of human/non-human collaboration. Custom robotic systems with computer vision, RNN, swarm behavior, and biofeedback capabilities.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: D.O.U.G._1 was built from open-source robotic arm plans found online, grounding the practice in open-source hardware. However, subsequent generations use increasingly custom/proprietary systems. Chung's conceptual framework and methodological approach is widely shared through talks, publications, and educational engagement. Scilicet studio collaborates with research institutions but the specific systems are not open-sourced.

governance_model.governance_detail: Solo artist with studio infrastructure. Scilicet studio (founded 2019) is led by Chung as founder and artistic director, working with collaborators across robotics, bio-sensing, and interspecies technology. The creative vision is singular but implementation involves collaborative teams. Institutional partnerships (WEF, V&A, MIT) involve shared project governance.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: D.O.U.G._3 (Collectivity) raises consent questions — trained on publicly available NYC surveillance footage, using movement data of unconsenting citizens. Other generations use the artist's own data (drawings, biometrics) with full self-consent. The practice explicitly questions what consent means in human-machine collaboration.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Machine co-authorship. Chung explicitly frames the robots as 'collaborators' rather than tools. The V&A acquired the RNN model itself as part of the artwork, recognizing the machine's contribution to authorship. Each D.O.U.G. generation explores a different authorship dynamic: mimicry, memory, collective, spectral.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Works are performative — they unfold in real-time as the artist and robots co-draw. Each performance is unique, driven by the artist's gestures, biometric data, or environmental inputs. D.O.U.G._4 responds to live EEG brainwave data. D.O.U.G._3 swarm robots respond to each other and to environmental conditions. The drawn outputs persist as material artifacts of the temporal process.

data_materiality.data_sources: Artist's own archived drawings (20 years, digitized and categorized for RNN training), live gesture data (computer vision), EEG brainwave data (biofeedback), NYC public surveillance footage (movement extraction for swarm training), VR drawing data (simulated environments).
data_materiality.data_provenance: Mixed. Artist's own drawings and biometrics are fully consented self-generated data. NYC surveillance footage is publicly available but captures unconsenting individuals' movements. VR data is self-generated in simulated environments.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: D.O.U.G._2 uses a recurrent neural network that learns a latent representation of the artist's drawing practice — effectively creating an embedding space of the artist's gestural vocabulary. The RNN generates new drawings by navigating this learned space. This represents direct engagement with embedding/latent space as artistic medium.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Yes — the practice spans drawing, painting, sculpture, performance, biosensing, and VR. The D.O.U.G. systems translate between modalities: brainwaves to gesture, gesture to mark, video to movement data.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Primary format is live performance — the artist drawing alongside robotic collaborators before an audience. Installations display the robotic systems alongside resulting artworks. Sculptures (3D printed from drawing data) and prints serve as material artifacts. Exhibited/performed at World Economic Forum, V&A London, MIT Media Lab, MoMA, and international venues.

interoperability.composability: Moderate. The D.O.U.G. systems accept various inputs (gesture, drawing data, EEG, surveillance data) and produce outputs (drawings, paintings, data). The multi-generational architecture suggests composability between different interaction protocols. However, the systems are not designed for external integration.
interoperability.technical_openness: Hybrid. D.O.U.G._1 built from open-source plans. Later generations are increasingly custom and proprietary. Conceptual framework is shared publicly but specific implementations are not open-sourced.

technical_approach.stack: Custom robotic arm systems (originally open-source plans), computer vision (color tracking, gesture analysis), recurrent neural networks (RNN for drawing generation), EEG biosensors, swarm robotics, VR headsets and simulated drawing environments, 3D printing, custom software for robotic control and data processing

network_position.scene_affiliation: Bridges contemporary art, AI/robotics research, performance art, and technology ethics communities. Connected to MIT Media Lab (former research affiliate), World Economic Forum (AI governance discussions), V&A (institutional collection), TIME100 AI list, and the broader human-machine collaboration art community.
network_position.connections: MIT Media Lab community, TIME100 AI cohort, V&A collection context, WEF AI governance community, broader robotic/AI art practitioners, Scilicet studio collaborators

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Chung's practice is the most direct living example of relational composition as primary medium — the feedback loop between human and machine agents generating art. Their exploration of machine co-authorship, data provenance (what data trains the collaborator?), and the ethics of human-machine creative relationships directly addresses questions A(DAI) must navigate. Their experience building successive generations of collaborative protocols (each D.O.U.G. as a different relational model) provides practical knowledge for designing human-AI creative infrastructure. Potential artwork-in-graph contributor or advisory voice on machine co-authorship.
